opus-5.5.text:
I think the word "pragmatic" really captures it. When we started Galbot, we asked a simple question: where can a general-purpose robot actually create value in the next few years, not in some distant future? And when you look at the real scenarios — retail stores, pharmacies, factory floors, warehouses — the ground is almost always flat. You don't need to climb stairs or walk over rubble to restock a shelf or move a box from one station to another.

So legs, in many of these settings, add a lot of cost and complexity without adding much capability. A bipedal robot has to spend enormous effort just staying balanced. That affects safety, it affects battery life, it affects reliability. If a legged robot loses power, it falls. A wheeled base just stops. For a robot working next to people in a store, that difference matters a lot.

The wheeled base also gives you a very stable platform for the upper body, and the upper body is where most of the value is. The hard problem in embodied intelligence is manipulation: grasping thousands of different objects, opening drawers, handling deformable things. We wanted to put our engineering effort and our compute budget into the hands, the arms, and the brain that controls them, rather than into locomotion.

Then there's cost and scale. If you want robots deployed in hundreds or thousands of locations, the bill of materials, the maintenance, and the uptime all matter. Wheels are mature, cheap, and robust. That lets us get robots into real environments sooner, and real deployment generates real data, which feeds back into the models. That flywheel is, in my view, the most important thing for this industry right now.

None of this means legs are wrong. For some scenarios, like homes with stairs or outdoor terrain, legs will eventually matter. But choosing a form factor is about matching the hardware to the problem you're solving today. For us, wheels plus dexterous dual arms was the fastest path to robots that are actually useful, and that's what I mean by pragmatic.

r001.rationale: The response says legs add cost and complexity and that engineering effort should focus on manipulation, but it does not argue that choosing highly immature hardware for an initial product impedes robot intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls wheels mature, cheap, and robust, but does not identify prior production at scale as evidence of component reliability.

r003.rationale: It says a legged robot falls if it loses power, but does not explain the broader claim that failure of any single component can disable the whole robot.

r004.rationale: The response says wheels help get robots deployed sooner, but does not argue that aggressive hardware choices can delay commercialization.

r005.rationale: It discusses matching hardware to the problem and the value of manipulation, but does not state that B2B customers prioritize task performance over legs versus wheels.

r006.rationale: It discusses uptime and deployment at many locations, but does not distinguish sustained customer deployment reliability demands from those of a brief demonstration.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because we're building a company, not a demo. When we started Galbot, the question I kept asking myself was: what can actually be deployed, at scale, in the next two or three years, and generate real value for customers? If you look at it that way, legs are a very expensive answer to a question most customers aren't asking.

Think about the environments where general-purpose robots will first make money. Pharmacies, retail stores, warehouses, factories, hospitals. These are overwhelmingly flat floors. Maybe there's a small ramp, maybe an elevator, but you don't need to climb stairs to restock a shelf or pick an order. So for the vast majority of early commercial scenarios, a wheeled base gets you ninety-plus percent of the mobility you need, at a fraction of the cost and complexity.

And complexity matters more than people realize. A bipedal humanoid has to spend an enormous amount of its engineering budget, its compute, its battery, just staying upright. Every step is a balance problem. If it falls in a store, that's a safety incident and possibly a broken robot worth hundreds of thousands of yuan. A wheeled platform doesn't fall over. It can run for a whole shift. It can carry a heavier payload. Your reliability numbers go up dramatically, and reliability is what a customer actually buys.

Our bet from day one has been that the real bottleneck for embodied AI isn't locomotion, it's manipulation. The hard problem is the hands and arms, and the brain behind them. Can the robot see a cluttered shelf, understand what's there, grasp an object it has never seen, and put it in the right place, thousands of times without failing? That's where the frontier is. So we deliberately took the mobility problem off the table, used a form that's mature and cheap, and poured our resources into the dual-arm system, the hands, and the large models driving them.

I'd also say we designed the body to be practical in a very literal sense. Our robot can lower itself to the floor and extend upward to reach a top shelf. A human-proportioned biped can't easily do that. So in some ways, for these tasks, the wheeled form isn't a compromise, it's actually better than the human form.

That said, I want to be clear: I'm not against legs. Long term, if you want a robot that goes into every home, that climbs stairs, legs will matter, and we're tracking that technology closely. But the sequence matters. First you prove the brain and the hands can do useful work, you get the data flywheel going with real deployments, and then you can put that intelligence onto whatever body the next scenario requires. Choosing wheels now is how we get to that future faster, not a decision to avoid it.

r001.rationale: The response says bipedal robots spend engineering resources on balance and that Galbot redirected effort toward manipulation, but it does not identify the hardware as highly immature or clearly connect immaturity to slower progress on intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls wheeled platforms mature and cheap, but gives no evidence of prior production at scale as a basis for reliability.

r003.rationale: It notes that a biped can fall and that a wheeled platform avoids falling, but does not explain how failure of any single component can disable the whole robot.

r004.rationale: It argues that legs add cost and complexity, emphasizes near-term customer deployment, and says choosing wheels now gets Galbot to that future faster.

r005.rationale: It says reliability is what customers buy and describes flat-floor tasks, but does not clearly state that B2B customers prioritize task performance over whether a robot has legs or wheels.

r006.rationale: It contrasts building a deployable company with building a demo, and says the wheeled robot can run a whole shift and serve real customer deployments.

astra-6.text:
I see it as pragmatic because the hardware should serve the task. If a robot is working on a relatively flat floor, wheels can provide mobility with less mechanical complexity and lower energy consumption than legs. That lets you focus more effort on manipulation—getting the robot to perceive objects, grasp them, and complete useful work reliably.

There are trade-offs: wheels limit where you can go, especially around stairs and uneven terrain. But you don’t have to solve every environment at once. For me, the practical question is whether the robot can deliver value consistently in the environments you’re targeting.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss immature hardware or how it could impede progress on robot intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not cite prior production at scale as evidence of component reliability.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that failure of any single component can disable the whole robot.

r004.rationale: It does not say that aggressive hardware choices can delay commercialization.

r005.rationale: It says hardware should serve the task, but does not identify B2B customers or state that they prioritize task performance over legs versus wheels.

r006.rationale: It does not distinguish reliability expectations for sustained customer deployment from those for a brief demonstration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the pragmatic part is choosing hardware around what the robot needs to do. If the task is to move around a relatively flat indoor space, pick things up, and carry them somewhere, wheels give you a simpler base. You don’t have to solve legged locomotion before you can start delivering value.

That lets you put more effort into perception, manipulation, and getting the whole system to work reliably. There are environments where legs would be useful, especially when you have stairs or uneven terrain. But you don’t need to solve every environment at once. You can start with the places where a wheeled robot is useful and expand from there.
